Industry News: AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium.
  • Sources indicate that "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW.
  • Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

Sources indicate that "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Recent findings suggest that jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

Franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is right now teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Industry observers note that even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

According to recent reports, "Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments.".

Recent findings suggest that with participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, stated class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

Sources indicate that 91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

It has been revealed that the last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

In a recent development, german politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students.".

Sources indicate that that's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

Recent findings suggest that german teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she mentioned.

There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular.".

Recent findings suggest that both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Sources indicate that müller noted one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

The Original Article was published on 24 June 2026.

Retraction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10702-5 Published online 24 June 2026.

According to recent reports, the authors retract this article, following a suggestion from the editors. Shortly after publication, a preprint (subsequently published (see ref. 1 below)) by Till Sawala identified an inconsistency in our analysis. Our calculations were erroneously comparing the comoving distance between the observed galaxies to the luminosity distance between galaxies in the simulated mocks. Correcting these concerns reduces the discrepancy between the observed and simulated samples to 1.48–2.75 sigma, depending on the sample construction. This falls below the standard significance threshold of 3 sigma in the cosmology literature.

Despite the revised uncertainties, our method remains valid and provides tentative evidence for anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of galaxies in the Universe. The revised paper, with corrected uncertainties, will be submitted to another journal. This retraction will contain a link to the new publication, if and when it is published.

Both authors agree with this retraction.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Football Association has registered interest in England hosting the Nations League finals.
  • On Sunday, the Three Lions booked their place as one of the top seeds in the newly expanded quarter-finals of the competition, beating world champions Spain to set up a clash against a second seed in March.
  • And England could well be playing a semi on home soil, if the FA has anything to do with it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Football Association has registered interest in England hosting the Nations League finals.

On Sunday, the Three Lions booked their place as one of the top seeds in the newly expanded quarter-finals of the competition, beating world champions Spain to set up a clash against a second seed in March.

And England could well be playing a semi on home soil, if the FA has anything to do with it.

According to Sami Mokbel of the BBC, England, Spain and France have all contacted UEFA, expressing their desire to host the final four games of next summer's Nations League competition.

The competition began in 2019, with the inaugural finals both hosted and ultimately won by Portugal, before heading to Italy (2021), the Netherlands (2023), and, most recently, Germany (2025).

England will face one of Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in the last eight of the competition – and could well become the first host of the finals not to reach the final four, given the new format of the competition.

So far, the only publically declared events at Wembley this June are two concerts from Newcastle United fan, Sam Fender, though these are scheduled to take place after the Nations League is due to be played.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

FourFourTwo understands that the FA would welcome the opportunity to host a mini-tournament with the European Championship coming to the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland in 2028 – with other venues in consideration for hosting duties next summer.

While the Etihad Stadium is booked for much of June for Oasis's Live '27 tour, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium is, so far, free to host, with cult noughties emo band Fall Out Boy and stadium rock veterans U2 booked either side of when the semi-finals would take place.

The Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool, meanwhile, could well host its first major internationals.

This isn't a new conundrum for the FA to solve, with the Community Shield recently affected by Wembley's commitments beyond football.

This summer, the season's curtain-raiser was held in Cardiff at the Millennium Stadium, while 2022 saw Erling Haaland make his Manchester City debut at the King Power Stadium in the fixture.

England will play home and away in the next international break in the Nations League quarter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Arsenal head coach Renee Slegers admitted her side had been outmuscled by a clinical Lyon side after a 2-0 defeat at Borehamwood dented hopes of direct qualification for the Champions League quarter-finals.

Lyon were yet to concede a goal in Europe this season and had won all of their nine domestic league matches so far.

The French side made the most of a bright start to take a 24th-minute lead through Jule Brand, and should have gone into half-time with a bigger advantaged but Marie-Antoinette Katoto – top scorer in the Champions League this season with seven goals – blazed over from six yards.

Although Arsenal were improved early in the second half, with Caitlin Foord stretching Lyon down the flanks, clear chances were still hard to come by.

Lyon added a second against the run of play in the 57th minute when Melchie Dumornay drilled a shot into the top corner following another blistering counter attack.

“It was a tough game, it was a challenge,” Slegers noted, quoted on the Arsenal club website.

“Especially the first half, also parts of the second half, the game becomes what they are good at, it was physical, it was fast. They are clinical with their moments, you see the quality they have.

“The second half, we dominated the game better, in possession, spent more time in their half, (but) still didn’t create clear cut chances.”.

Arsenal – who had battled to a 1-1 draw at holders Barcelona last time out – slipped to a first European defeat this season and ended the night in eighth place.

Lyon sit joint top with Barcelona on 13 points and already assured of a place in the quarter-finals ahead of the final round of league stage games.

Arsenal will be away to Inter Milan and could yet still avoid having to go into the play-off round if other results also go their way.

In a recent development, “It is the three points in Milan, that is everything we can control,” Slegers remarked. “That is what we go for, and then we will see what the other teams do.”.

#13683. Swing when you’re winning? Biggest leaps across Fifa’s football rankings | The Knowledge

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1566 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Swing when you’re winning? Biggest leaps across Fifa’s football rankings | The Knowledge

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more.
  • “The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic.
  • Recent findings suggest that the gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more.

Mail us with all of your questions and answers.

“The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic. “Is this the biggest gap between the best and worst ranking for one national team?”.

Recent findings suggest that the gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles. And, as Chris Lewis and others point out, there are a couple of other home nations who have had more dramatic swings. Wales and Northern Ireland both moved up 109 places: Wales from 117th to eighth under Gary Speed and then Chris Coleman, Northern Ireland from 129th in 2004 to 20th in 2017.

Recent findings suggest that it is the speed of Scotland’s improvement that was most notable. “At two years, seven months and one day that feels like quite the rise,” writes Robbie Dale. “A look at the data demonstrates it is bettered by only nine other countries. Colombia’s rise from a low of 51 to a high of 12 in exactly two years [between 2016 and 2018] is one notable example. Dominica and Kenya rose up the ranks by 70 and 69 places respectively over the course of just 16 months.”.

Some of the biggest movers are countries who joined Fifa after the men’s rankings were introduced in 1992, which means they started at the bottom. “I immediately thought of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” writes JJ Galbraith. “They were ranked 173rd in 1996, shortly after playing their first game as an independent nation. Their pinnacle was 13th place in 2013 – a rise of 160 places.”.

It has been revealed that that 160-place gap is beaten by only two teams. Kuwait reached 24th in the Fifa rankings in 1998, when they won the Arabian Gulf Cup in style and finished second at the Asian Games. By 2017 they were 189th in the world, a difference of 165 places.

According to recent reports, that is 18 places short of the record. “Montenegro were ranked 199th when they played their first international match in 2007,” writes Pete Tomlin. “In 2011 they managed to climb up to 16th, thanks to some strong results in Euro 2012 qualifying (victories against Wales, Bulgaria and Switzerland and a 0-0 draw with England at Wembley).”.

Thanks to Pete, Mark Holt, Cameron McGlone, Sean DeLoughry and others for helping us compile this list of the biggest movers.

183 places Montenegro (16th/199th).

160 Bosnia and Herzegovina (13/173).

153 Central African Republic (49/202).

136 Cuba (46/182), Slovakia (14/150).

Recent findings suggest that pete Tomlin has also crunched the numbers for the women’s game. “The gaps are much smaller,” writes Pete, “due to the fact that the rankings have only been recorded since 2003, there are fewer teams and many of the national sides play very few matches.

According to recent reports, “The biggest gap belongs to the Bahamas with a high of 96th and a low of 194th, a difference of 98 places. There are actually two women’s teams with a gap of zero, but this is because they have played so few games. Chad (156th) and Sudan (194th) have never moved.”.

“Non-league minnows Plymouth Parkway reached the second round of the FA Cup the other weekend,” writes Jon Archer. “I noticed their club crest appears to feature a road going under a bridge. Are there any other clubs who have roads on their badge?” Indeed the Southern League Premier Division South side have the A38 on their crest, a nod to, erm, the nearby stretch of dual carriageway that helps give the club its name via their former ground at the Parkway Sports Club.

It is not a common occurrence and somewhat depends on how far you want to stretch things. Sunderland, for example, have a section of the Wearmouth Bridge on their crest, which certainly carries a road, though it is not visible. Similarly National League South’s Maidenhead United redesigned their badge in 2020 to celebrate the club’s 150th anniversary – it features a stretch of the town’s Thames river bridge, a nod to where the club played their first game back in 1870, which now carries the A4. Farther afield the German minnows TSG Backnang’s crest features the Murr Valley viaduct, which both overlooks the team’s ground and carries the B14, which links Stuttgart and Nuremberg.

Those might be a bit of a reach, but, far more definitively, across the West Country from Plymouth Parkway are tiny eighth-tier Willand Rovers of the Southern League Division One South. Their badge is a proper old shield effort featuring the River Culm, a castle tower … and the M5 motorway, which slices through the village to the north.

Industry observers note that “Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

The answers above put Liverpool on two titles per manager and their great rivals down the M62 on 6.66 titles per manager (which is doing Alex Ferguson a great disservice but we have to find a way to make this question work). Daz Pearce offers up one-title-one-manager wonders Leicester (Claudio Ranieri), Nottingham Forest (Brian Clough) and Ipswich (Alf Ramsey) for the most managers per title. We would need a team winning only one title in their history in a season with two different managers to get lower than 1:1 but Dirk Maas has a more impressive example of a team with one manager per title.

“Since the inception of the Eredivisie in 1956, Feyenoord have secured 11 league titles, won by 11 managers: Jiri Sobotka in 1961, Franz Fuchs in 1962, Wilhelm Kment in 1965, Ben Peeters in 1969, Ernst Happel in 1971, Wiel Coerver in 1974, Thijs Libregts in 1984, Willem van Hanegem in 1993, Leo Beenhakker in 1999, Giovanni van Bronckhorst in 2017 and Arne Slot in 2023.” Alex Ferguson’s haul of 13 league titles over his 26 years in the Manchester United dugout makes United’s titles-per-manager ratio hard to beat and, probably, the definitive answer for fewest managers per title. Rangers have won 55 Scottish league titles with only nine managers for 6.11 titles per manager. That is as close as we could get. If you know of a club with a higher number of titles per manager, get in touch at knowledge@theguardian.com.

“It dawned on me recently that if Chelsea were to go on and win the Europa League this year on 15 May that, for a period of 10 days, they would be the holders of both major European trophies (as well as being technically the holders of the Cup Winners’ Cup),” wrote Brian Quinn in March 2013. “Has there ever been another brief period like this when a team held two European honours simultaneously? Perhaps going back to when there were three distinct European competitions?”.

Chelsea will indeed claim a unique honour if they triumph at the Amsterdam Arena in May (spoiler alert: they did). Only four sides have ever won different European competitions in consecutive years – Juventus, Milan, Porto and Liverpool – and in each instance the teams were deposed as holders of one trophy before getting their hands on the other.

Milan won the much-missed Cup Winners’ Cup on 23 May 1968, but Slovan Bratislava were crowned the upcoming champions on 21 May 1969, seven days before Milan hammered Ajax in the Bernabéu to win the 1969 European Cup. Similarly Juventus won the Cup Winners’ Cup on 16 May 1984, but Everton won that tournament almost exactly a year later on 15 May 1985, a fortnight before Juventus won the European Cup in a final overshadowed by the Heysel tragedy.

Likewise, Porto fell a week short in 2002-03 and 2003-04 after winning the Uefa Cup then the Champions League under José Mourinho, as did Liverpool between their Uefa Cup and European Cup wins in 1975-76 and 1976-77.

“Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, on Sunday. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?”.

Industry observers note that “Against the Netherlands this week, Florian Wirtz scored one goal that went in off a post and one that went in off the crossbar. Has anyone ever gone one better and scored a hat-trick with a goal off each post and one off the crossbar?” wonders David Hagan.

Recent findings suggest that “Seeing Cuba thrash Grenada 9-0 in the Concacaf Nations League, I noted there were eight different scorers (Jorge Aguirre scoring twice). Has any team gone better?” asks Oliver Tuhey.

“My team, Tranmere Rovers, have appeared at Wembley nine times since 1990,” writes David Carruthers. “Can any other team never to have played in the top division beat this?”.

“Are Leicester City the quickest team ever to go from winning the FA Cup to playing in the FA Cup first round proper?” asks Ricardio Sentulio.

Mail us with all of your questions and answers.

Arsenal winger Bukayo Saka is facing another month on the sidelines as he continues to recover from a thigh injury, taking his absence to eight weeks.

Saka picked up the injury early in a Champions League game against Bayern Munich on 21 October.

Manager Mikel Arteta issued the enhancement at a press conference ahead of the Premier League’s return, with Arsenal heading to Newcastle for their first game since the international break.

Arteta noted Saka had undergone more tests on the matter and was “evolving really well”.

Industry observers note that he remarked: “It looks like it’s going to be an eight-week injury, more or less, so I think it’s four at the moment. Still a while before he's back with the team.”.

Arsenal will also be missing midfielder Martin Zubimendi for a “few weeks” after he picked up a hamstring injury with Spain during the Nations League break, but the Gunners were handed a boost with centre-back William Saliba finally available for selection after a lengthy absence.

The Frenchman has been struggling with a back injury which he was managing at the end of the 2025-26 campaign, and it brought his World Cup to a premature end as he was forced off half an hour into France’s semi-final defeat.

But he did not require surgery and after several months out, has now played two practice matches and is set to be included in the squad.

According to recent reports, arteta mentioned: “He's ready. He's in a good condition. He played two games, one behind closed doors and one more official and he did really well and he's in good condition.

“We want to ramp up his minutes.”.

In a recent development, on Zubimendi, Arteta said: “He's out. Unfortunately he has a slight problem in his hamstring. He wasn't too concerned after the game but after the MRI scan revealed there's an injury there and he's going to be out for a few weeks.”.

Arteta also responded to the idea that Fantasy Premier League (FPL) selections by top-flight players, staff and family members have contributed towards team news leaks in recent weeks.

He said: “It's a topic. This is the kind of things that are happening in our society right now and it's something new, we haven't dealt with it and we have to put new things in place.

Recent findings suggest that “The confidentiality is something critical because it's about trust and what you're trying to do and that should be kept as a huge secret. And we will take measures to make sure that doesn't happen.”.

#13677. Industry News: Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1048 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal.
  • But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
  • As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.

But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.

As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.

They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).

Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.

The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.

Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find fresh forms of income.

A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.

Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.

It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.

"I think it's more of a long-term game," said Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.

According to recent reports, she indicates it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it shows it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.

One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels.".

She says it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF intends and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.

The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott said.

This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.

Since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national intends to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no newly introduced commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.

Kumar says more countries could announce similar looks just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.

Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.

Industry observers note that the nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.

The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.

According to recent reports, the roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.

Kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.

This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any big announcements about fossil fuels.

Global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.

A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald shows that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing new reserves.

Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.

One issue Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.

The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.

Ideally, Kumar said, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.

"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum.".

#13673. ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1168 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of new research and guidelines for pregnant players.
  • Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.
  • Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of new research and guidelines for pregnant players.

Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

Sources indicate that “I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” says 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”.

For many years, notes the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa debuted its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

Sources indicate that “I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” indicates Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

It has been revealed that “Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”.

Industry observers note that up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, states Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

“More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she notes. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

Sources indicate that “There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour claims. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”.

It has been revealed that some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

When Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she notes. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”.

Though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she says. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

But for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie states candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”.

Industry observers note that the other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she says bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a latest deal being offered.

Even so, Dufour claims, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data demonstrates that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an crucial fact.

#13672. Breaking: The last golden era of the Premier League is long gone: Why 2004-16 was the best of the Barclays

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1101 w)
📖 Baca

Breaking: The last golden era of the Premier League is long gone: Why 2004-16 was the best of the Barclays

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the so-called “Best League in the World™”, it’s safe to say the Premier League is currently experiencing a full-blown existential crisis.
  • It has been revealed that the bombshell announcement of Manchester City’s guilt on all but one of their 115 charges has left the game feeling more hollow than ever before.
  • So with that, let’s cast our minds to a simpler, purer time, the much-fabled “Barclays era” of 2004 to 2016.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the so-called “Best League in the World™”, it’s safe to say the Premier League is currently experiencing a full-blown existential crisis.

It has been revealed that the bombshell announcement of Manchester City’s guilt on all but one of their 115 charges has left the game feeling more hollow than ever before. Is there a title race? Who’s going down? What is real? Does any of this mean anything? Throw in the continued abomination that is VAR and more, and it’s all just a bit bleak.

So with that, let’s cast our minds to a simpler, purer time, the much-fabled “Barclays era” of 2004 to 2016.

While football didn’t start in 1992, the Premier League did and by the early-to-mid 2000s, it was reaching its apex as the blood and thunder of decades prior fused with the new-found flair and panache to create a near-perfect concoction.

The current state of the English top-flight can be traced all the way back to the summer of 2003 with Roman Abramovich’s purchase of Chelsea. It was the moment the horse bolted and nothing has been the same since.

Industry observers note that however, at the time, it was all just a little bit exciting and things really picked up 12 months later when Jose Mourinho landed in West London, rightly claiming to be the “Special One”. The reigning European Cup winner was joined by Rafael Benitez, who came to Liverpool after incredible success with Valencia.

Recent findings suggest that suddenly, Sir Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger were no longer the only gunslingers in town. The “Substantial Two” quickly became the “Big Four” as Mourinho romped to the league title - breaking numerous records - and Benitez amazingly won the Champions League. Istanbul and all that.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

According to recent reports, the two Iberians changed so much in the English game. From how to set up a side to how to win the title - 4-4-2 and peaking after Christmas being swapped out for 4-3-3 and rapid-fast starts.

It has been revealed that liverpool’s fifth European Cup was significant for numerous reasons. It was their first in 21 years but also the first final featuring an English side in the 21st century. They had beaten Chelsea to get there, starting both an incredible rivalry between the clubs and managers, and a golden age for the Premier League.

Over the next four years, all of the then-”Big Four” made finals and there were three semi-finalists in every season from 06/07 to 08/09. The peak came in 2008 when each was knocked out by another with United eventually toppling Chelsea in the first all-English final in Moscow. In one of the odder paradoxes, England failed to qualify for the European Championships that summer.

Sources indicate that fergie’s empire had struck back with Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney at the forefront of it. In an era of elite pairings, there was no finer. Ronaldo’s Ballon d’Or win confirmed his status as the best player in the world, and the Premier League as truly the best league.

Sources indicate that it was also a time of far less financial disparity with the rest of Europe, Milan and Inter lifting the Champions League in 2007 and 2010 respectively. Things would soon change and not for the better.

While the big boys competed for the biggest trophies, there were plenty of brilliant stories elsewhere. Harry Redknapp’s Portsmouth won the FA Cup in 2008, setting the tone for Wigan five years later in epic fashion against City months on from Swansea claiming the League Cup. Only Crystal Palace's success in 2025 has been comparable since.

Throw in Major Sam’s Bolton, Blackburn, Stoke, Hull and others and it was the last definitive age of the cult teams and cult heroes, or as they’ve become better known - The Barclaysmen. With the overload of data nowadays, another Michu-like madness feels further away than ever.

Abu Dhabi’s takeover of City in 2008 is the obvious place to pinpoint the beginning of the end, but Mourinho’s first Chelsea exit a year prior and Ronaldo’s first from United a year after moved the centre of attention from England to Spain.

While European success faded - a fate-like Chelsea were the only winners from 2008 to 2019 - there were still memorable domestic moments, two of which unfortunately led to City winning their first pair of Premier League titles. Agueroooooo and Gerrard’s slip may be rendered utterly irrelevant soon but the memories won’t. It was peak Premier League.

As was Sir Alex Ferguson’s last dance in 2013 and Leicester’s miracle title win in 2016, which will never be topped as the greatest achievement in the history of English football. That it came either side of Chelsea’s crooked titles and prior to City’s dodgy dominance makes it all the more appropriate as the ending of the last great era. And that goes for both in football and the world itself.

While the on-field action of the last decade may feel fraudulent, how we now consume football is also a far cry from those halcyon Barclays days.

Streaming was not yet a thing in 2004. Sky Sports was in its pomp. Super Sunday actually lived up to its billing as appointment viewing.

Influencers and content creators had not yet taken over. Gary Neville went past his winger on the overlap rather than host it. Social media was still fun for the most part.

We had Soccer AM and Goals on Sunday, Gillette Soccer Saturday and Match of the Day at elite levels, and even room for demonstrates like Wayne Rooney’s Street Striker and Football’s Next Star.

Nostalgia is a helluva drug, but as Independent Panels decide the fate of English football past, present and future, it’s near-impossible to dispute that, like so much of entertainment, we had it so much better before.

One day, the pendulum will hopefully swing back in our favour but, for now, a rewatch of Premier League Years on Sky may be in order.

Peter writes freelance for FourFourTwo and has previous experience at Evening Standard and Football365 among several others. He now works for us alongside OneFootball, the Sporting News and Stats Perform. One of the very few Irish people living in London and even fewer to support Manchester United, he spends time away from football rewatching TV reveals and attempting to play tennis.

Archie Gray will make his first appearance against his old club today after joining Spurs from Leeds in 2024. He was an unused sub in the two matches last season but is now an established part of this De Zerbi resurgence, starting all but two matches in the current campaign. Gray was named in the England Under-21 squad yesterday but is heading in the right direction for a senior call-up.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin is starting for Leeds today, after doubts over a foot issue heading into the Elland Road fixture. He was named in the England squad yesterday, which suggested he was not ruled out of this clash against Spurs.

Roberto De Zerbi has kept a settled team as he looks to make it four Premier League wins in a row. Dominic Solanke is dropped to the bench in his only change, with Pedro Porro coming in – so it may be Omar Marmoush playing as a central forward.

It has been revealed that there are many processes in [Tottenham’s] build-up. You need players to interpret this and the legs to cover the centre of the game. It is always complicated [tactically against a De Zerbi team], very dominant in possession. You have to find solutions to be competitive in this area.

According to recent reports, the most important thing is what happens on the pitch but [we have bought] Sean [in because of the] tactical aspect. He is sop smart, has experience and also the legs to compete. It’s necessary to have a third midfielder on the pitch to control their processes. On the other hand he is sharp on the offensive actions, many times. Lukas [Nmecha] brings the greediness, physicality and can take the attention off Dominic. he has been very sharp in training, scoring many goals and for that he has the chance to shine today.

Dominic is a key player and thank God he was able to join us in team training yesterday. Overall he is in a good position.

You will always have spells in the Premier League when you cannot convert good performances into results or when you can’t score many goals. We are struggling with injuries for key players in our attack – Noah Okafor, Anton Stach – but hopefully we have also turned the corner.

The pre-season, it was clear [he is] a special talent. You recognise the special talent immediately and he doesn’t need to show something special, you understand? Everything that he does and he is one of the special talents.

The next step he has to enjoy, he has to follow the older players, the players with more experience like [Andrew] Robertson, [James] Maddison, Ben Davies and to find the time to play.

It is my responsibility because when you manage young players and sucho major talents like Luca, it is a bigger responsibility for me.

He has to be ready when he goes on the pitch. I think it [does] not depend on the result, he can play from the beginning. Before the Chelsea game, I thought to play with him in the first XI, but in the end you have to find the right moment and for them also.

I think the age is not so crucial. The most important is the quality, personality, the behaviour on the pitch and the qualities. And Luca has all of these qualities.

Industry observers note that leeds United are heartbroken to learn of the passing of supporter Colin Westby at the age of 68. Colin suffered a medical emergency ahead of our Premier League fixture with Manchester United on Sunday 18 October at Elland Road. After being transferred to hospital, he was placed into a medically induced coma and sadly following a period of unresponsiveness, the decision was made to withdraw life support. Colin was a long-standing Season Ticket Holder at the club, attending matches for over 50 years. The thoughts of everyone at Leeds United are with Colin's family and friends at this sad time. We will pay tribute to Colin in the 68th minute of our next Premier League fixture with Tottenham Hotspur, on Saturday 7 November.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Leeds United and Tottenham Hotspur at Elland Road. The home side, lions at night and mice in the morning, have the unenviable record of 21 top-flight matches with a kick-off time before 3pm without a win. All that extra TV moolah comes in handy but their home ground, a bearpit under the floodlights, is neutered when its denizens are yawning instead of being fired up by social lubricant.

In a recent development, daniel Farke’s team started the campaign well but are now without a win in five, drawing three matches with teams beneath them in the table – Crystal Palace, Manchester United and Sunderland – and  losing to two above them, Arsenal and Bournemouth. In fairness they played well against the champions for an hour and were deservedly in the lead until Mikel Arteta turnd to his billionaire’s bench and changed the game. At Bournemouth last week they also made a decent start, had a goal disallowed for striking Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s arm and then James Trafford chucked one in.

Industry observers note that they never recovered, found themselves increasingly bogged down when trying to unlock a low block and were mugged on the break in added time to lose 2-0. They are a robust side overly reliant on their wing-backs to create chances for their No 9 in the absence of the injured Noah Okafor who was unavailable to train with the team this week because of a groin injury but may be fit enough for the bench.

Sources indicate that spurs, by contrast, are buoyant following three wins on the bounce – over Coventry, Chelsea and Palace, two with clean sheets – that has taken them from 19th to ninth, three places above Leeds. They have won their last three visits to Elland Road, 0-4 under Antonio Conte, which proved to be the last match of Marcelo Bielsa’s glorious spell at the Peacocks, 1-4 under Ryan Mason, which sealed Leeds’ relegation, and 1-2 under Tomas Frank last year by virtue of goals from Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus as the home side struggled against their width back in the days before their switch to a back three.

According to recent reports, tel also scored in Spurs’ home game, a 1-1 draw in May, and then kicked Ethan Ampadu in the head to concede the penalty from which Leeds equalised. I wonder what kind of impact he will have today. Incidentally Roberto De Zerbi on his last visit to Leeds when manager of Brighton in 2022-23 had such a strop on the touchline when the home team equalised that he was within a gnat’s whisker of being sent off.

Follow latest updates from the quarter-final draw below:.

England will play Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals in March, in a rematch of their World Cup quarter-final.

Jude Bellingham scored twice in Miami as England came from behind to end Norway’s sensational World Cup run back in July.

But Erling Haaland’s team will be out for revenge after their incredible comeback to beat Denmark secured progress to the two-legged Nations League quarter-finals.

The Three Lions, who topped Group A3 with a 3-2 win over world champions Spain, will travel to Oslo in the first leg before hosting the second leg as they bid to reach the Nations League Finals in June.

Should England progress to the semi-finals, they will play either Jurgen Klopp’s Germany or Belgium, while the other semi-final will see either Spain or France play against Portugal or the Netherlands.

In the Nations League play-offs, which were also decided during the draw in Nyon, Wales will play Slovenia as they bid to retain their top-tier status.

The Republic of Ireland face a tough test against Croatia as they attempt to reach League A for the first time. Both ties will be played across two legs, also in March.

Norway will be out for revenge against England, who could face Jurgen Klopp’s Germany if they reach the semi-finals.

England have been handed a suspended ban for away supporters as a result of “racist and/or discriminatory behaviour” by fans during Sunday’s 3-2 win over Spain in Madrid.

The ban, which would apply to one match, is suspended for a period of two years, meaning any similar offence during that period would enforce it.

The FA has also been fined €15,000 (£12,600).

The four Nations League quarter-finals will be played across two legs during the international break in March 2027.

The first legs will be played over the 25-27th March with the second legs played between 28-30th March.

The semi-finals and final will follow in June 2027 following the end of the 2026/27 domestic season.

Jurgen Klopp must be feeling confident about Germany’s chances of progressing further in the competition.

The German team haven’t been anywhere near their best so far but they’re drawn against an aging and rebuilding Beglium team in the quarter-finals.

Belgium managed to come through a pressure-filled contest against Italy in the group stage in a sign of their lasting quality but Germany will be favourites.

The Germans also have the added motivation of a possible semi-final with England to come so they should be firing on all cylinders come the quarter-finals in March.

In the third quarter-final the Netherlands will host Portugal.

Portugal have very fond memories of the Nations League having won the competition twice including the inaugural tournament.

They are also the reigning champions having beaten Spain in a penalty shootout last year.

Can the Netherlands muster up enough quality to overcome a Cristiano Ronaldo-less Portugal side and reach the final four?

Elsewhere the Nations League quarter-finals have also thrown up another World Cup rematch.

This one is from the semi-finals as Spain take on France once again.

Spain have won each of the last three knockout games against France with those coming in three different competitions.

They won 2-1 in the Euro 2024 semi-finals before a 5-4 victory in the Nations League semi-finals in 2025.

Most recently, of course, they won 2-0 in the World Cup semi-finals in a match they completely dominated.

Can France overcome them across two legs this time around?

England’s quarter-final tie against Norway will be a rematch of their meeting at this summer’s World Cup.

The Three Lions triumphed on that occasion with Jude Bellingham scoring twice to overturn Andreas Schjelderup’s opener and secure a 2-1 win after extra-time.

Norway were arguably the better team on the day though and will feel confident about challenging England over two-legs come March.

What does that mean for England?

Thomas Tuchel’s men will take on Norway in the quarter-finals.

Should they progress from that tie they will face either Germany or Belgium in the semi-finals.

If they reach the final they will play one of France, Spain, Portugal or the Netherlands.

Now, a draw is made to determine the semi-final fixtures.

In the first semi-final will be the winners of quarter-final three.

They will take on the winners of quarter-final one.

In the second semi-final the winners of quarter-final four will face the winners of two.

#13666. Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (985 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers.
  • Who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager?
  • Recent findings suggest that although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers.

Who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager? – Tom S.

Recent findings suggest that although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach. The 2030 World Cup is a long way away and I’m not sure the Concacaf Nations League, the Gold Cup or even the 2028 Copa América carry much appeal for a manager with European experience or aspirations. But I’m not entirely sure that sort of coach is necessarily a great idea. The last two World Cups, after all, have been won by low-key coaches who have come from within the federation and have worked with many of the players at youth level. That’s the positive from appointing from within; appointing from without is almost certainly more expensive and there’s the danger the next foreign manager does just what Mauricio Pochettino does, and has his head turned by the first vaguely attractive European job that comes calling.

The United States’ interest in Pep Guardiola, and his talks with Italy earlier, have me wondering – what separates club and international management? Could Pep, as successful as he’s been, do well in either? – Joe P.

Industry observers note that international and club management seem to me related but essentially different jobs. It’s one thing to have the players every day and be able to drill them over and over to impose a philosophy; quite another to pick them up for perhaps a dozen training sessions over a calendar year, plus major tournaments. International football is necessarily less sophisticated than club football, more based on individual excellence or heroism. Guardiola, you suspect, would be able to adapt, but it’s not certain. Plus there’s the fact that at major tournaments players are with their manager for a month or more, cooped up in the same hotel with no release. With the more intense coaches, such as Marcelo Bielsa, that seems to become problematic. And it’s notable that at the last World Cup the nations with the major-name managers – England, Brazil, the United States, Germany – fared less well than those who had appointed technocrats from within.

Sources indicate that michael Carrick’s firing highlighted the lack of top-class English managers. Why has an Englishman never managed a Premier League club to a title? – Ricky M.

I think there are two related problems here. Are there any good English coaches? To which the answer appears to be that there are nowhere near as many as there ought to be. The various changes in player development enacted by the elite player performance plan and the England DNA project have, over the past 10-15 years, led to the development of far more technically proficient English players than there have ever been before, which has been reflected in the uptick in England’s performances at major tournaments. St George’s Park was supposed to be about developing coaches as well as players but, as yet, that seems not to have happened.

Industry observers note that that mentioned, it’s probably also the case that it’s very hard for British coaches to be appointed to top Premier League jobs. Say they get their start at a mid-sized Championship club and win promotion; they then have to amend their approach in the Premier League to scrap for points in a relegation battle. If they fail they are written off as not good enough for the top division; if they succeed, they’re seen as not playing the right sort of football for an elite club. It’s happened to Scott Parker … even the likes of Gary O’Neil or Eddie Howe seem somehow not quite right for the elite who, perhaps understandably, prefer to turn to somebody with experience of European competition.

Is there any part of you that feels sympathy for the current Man City players, who will presumably have to play out a “lost season” thanks to actions they had nothing to do with, and which probably happened long before their time at the club? – Jason D.

To an extent, yes, but they’re pretty naïve if they didn’t realise the potential glitch they were walking into. I have far more sympathy for those players who played for clubs who were denied success by City’s cheating. It’s not just the teams who finished second in the league, lost to City in cup competitions or missed out on European qualification because of City; it’s those teams, most obviously Arsenal and Aston Villa, whose development was derailed by City taking their best players, offering wages and transfer fees that it turns out they had no business offering.

It has been revealed that italy have gotten some significant results in the Nations League. Are they back? – Nicholas A.

In a recent development, this question, to be fair, was sent in before the 4-1 defeat to Belgium on Sunday. But anyway, beating France at home may be a big result, but that and two wins over Turkey seems limited evidence to say they’re back. They have definitely looked sharper under Roberto Mancini than they have probably since winning the Euros under him five years ago, but that’s a long way from being back. Even if they were to win the Euros in 2028, it wouldn’t alter the fact they haven’t qualified for three World Cups in a row. They need to qualify for 2030 and then probably get to at least the quarter-finals before you can start to say they may be back. And even then, Serie A is way off what it was at its peak – and how many of this squad would get in a Spain or England squad? Even being generous, probably no more than four or five.

Antonio Conte has claimed clubs are 'frightened of winning' if they have concerns over his methods after the Italian was overlooked for the Manchester United job.

Conte had been heavily linked with the role at Old Trafford, joining Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe and Unai Emery among the list bookmakers' favourites to replace Michael Carrick.

Man United ultimately went with another former Chelsea and Tottenham boss in Mauricio Pochettino, paying around £10million in compensation to lure him away from being head coach of the United States' national team.

Conte, who remains out of work after leaving Napoli in the summer, has now hit back at reports suggesting Man United may have been put off by his intensity and demands.

'First, let me address the question of my method,' Conte told the Cronache di Spogliatoio podcast.

'If anyone is frightened by my method, then they are frightened of winning, because that methodology leads to victory. That is my answer.

Antonio Conte has claimed clubs are 'frightened of winning' if they have concerns over his methods after the Italian was overlooked for the Manchester United job.

Man United opted to appoint Mauricio Pochettino as head coach after sacking Michael Carrick.

Conte hit back at suggestions Man United's hierachy might have been relucant to appoint him because of his methods.

'Manchester United has such a significant history that I find it strange to imagine anyone could be afraid of an approach aimed at restoring the club to its true stature.

It has been revealed that '(United) last won the league in 2013, under Ferguson. I have immense respect for Sir Alex Ferguson.

'I've read his book, and when I was in London, I was fortunate enough to visit his home and spend a day with him. He has an incredible passion for talking about football, though, at times, his Scottish accent can be quite hard to follow.

'Through his own methodology and approach, he made Manchester United great.

'That is why I find certain remarks almost offensive toward United; it's as if someone were placing a veto on the club's return to its own history.

Recent findings suggest that 'A method is what's needed to achieve major results. And if you're suggesting that this method requires hard work, well, yes, it does. Everyone has to work hard, not just the players.'.

Conte has long been known for his combustible personality - as well as an impressive winning record as a coach.

In a recent development, at Chelsea, he fell out with star striker Diego Costa, centre back David Luiz and the club's board. At Napoli, he left a year after winning the Serie A title and said there was 'too much poison, too much malice' at the club.

Conte has developed a reputation for his high intensity and demands, while the Italian famously left Tottenham after an explosive press conference attacking the club's culture.

Conte has won five Serie A titles across three clubs and won the Premier League with Chelsea.

Conte famously left Tottenham after an explosive press conference in 2023, where he labelled his players as 'selfish' and took aim at the club's culture.

The Italian, however, has overseen five Serie A title wins during his spells at Juventus, Inter Milan and Napoli, along with winning the Premier League and FA Cup with Chelsea.

It is not the first time Conte has spoken out in recent weeks following links to Old Trafford, with the 57-year-old having denied he had set 'specific conditions' about taking over at United.

La Repubblica claimed Conte wanted 'carte blanche on the transfer market' and to act as a manager, rather than a head coach, with a technical staff behind the scenes chosen by him involving 'trusted collaborators'.

'My name has been linked with numerous clubs, but there are at the moment no negotiations at an advanced stage,' Conte responded on social media last month.

In a recent development, 'Following a wonderful and successful spell in charge of Napoli, I will take the time I need to consider how and when to return to management. It will be a carefully considered decision, one I will make when I believe the conditions are right.

According to recent reports, 'I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my "strong personality". These reports are unfounded, as there is presently no concrete basis for such assessments.

'Should a concrete opportunity arise, that will be the time to hold discussions with the club concerned and jointly consider the terms of a potential agreement, with due regard for both parties' needs and the qualities and approach that define my work as a manager.'.

Pochettino, who landed the job at Old Trafford, has faced a whirlwind start having flown into Manchester following his final match in charge of the United States on Tuesday.

The Argentine took training for the first time on Thursday and will lead the Red Devils out for the first time on Sunday in a blockbuster clash with Liverpool at Anfield.

Pochettino takes over with Man United lying in the Premier League's relegation zone having won just one of their opening ten matches.
